prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, bringing optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: B037 is the case in which the discovery and the people line up most cleanly. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice proposal and early demonstration, and Ye's group taking strontium lattice clocks to the 10^-18 regime with many-body and comb-linked extensions, are two identifiable and complementary contributions that fit a two-person prize without strain. The achievement has been reproduced and surpassed by several independent laboratories, it has enabled centimetre-scale tests of the gravitational redshift, limits on varying constants and dark-matter couplings, and it is the practical route to a redefinition of the second. Seven of eight members ranked it, three placed it in their top three and two placed it first, so it is the broadest first-or-second-tier support on the shortlist. My own opening ballot put the Higgs observation first, but the exchange of opening views has made me weigh more heavily that three colleagues independently describe the Higgs credit as arbitrary, whereas nobody calls the Katori-Ye credit unresolved. The committee identifies the discovery and then the people behind it, and here the second step is defensible.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty against recent precedent: the 2005 prize covered the frequency comb (and Ye was part of that circle of work) and the 2012 prize covered ion-based optical control and clocks, so a lattice-clock prize can be read as an incremental step within a field that has already been honoured. There is also the question whether the pending redefinition of the second should come first, and whether other contributors to optical clock accuracy (ion-clock and Al+ groups, NIST and PTB teams) are being passed over. Separately, from my own position as a theorist working on quantum gravity and cosmology, I am less able than Lindroth or Kroll to judge the finer experimental priority history, and I have to rely on their reading of it. If those concerns prove decisive, the Higgs observation (B006) remains the more fundamental discovery, and I would not want a precision-metrology prize to displace it without the committee having faced its attribution problem openly.

responses.point: On B006 Eriksson accepts that the Higgs discovery is scientifically clear and mature, but argues that the three-laureate limit cannot fairly represent thousands of contributors and that choosing spokespersons or proponents is inherently arbitrary; he also notes the 2013 prize already recognised the mechanism.
responses.response: I put B006 first in my opening ballot and I now concede most of this. The credited names are founders and project leaders of ATLAS and CMS, not the people who made the 2012 observation, and I said then that I could not verify whether detector leadership is the right proxy. Eriksson's point sharpens it: a prize would have to defend, against every other plausible choice of three, why these three, and I cannot do that from the supplied evidence. I do not agree that the 2013 prize reduces the urgency, since the mechanism and its observation are different achievements, which is why I keep B006 as an alternative rather than dropping it. But I no longer think the committee can be expected to resolve its attribution problem this year, and I have moved B037 above it.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B037 first as a clean laser-spectroscopy breakthrough with a fair two-name credit, while noting that the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-trap prize may lead some members to see it as incremental, and that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened.
responses.response: I agree with the core of the assessment and with the two-name credit, and I want to answer the incrementalism worry directly. The 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured the comb and the control of single trapped ions; neither contains the idea that many neutral atoms held at the magic wavelength can be interrogated at once without light-shift penalty, which is what delivers the stability and accuracy gain and what makes relativistic geodesy and the dark-matter and constants searches possible. That is a distinct achievement. Where I would qualify Kroll is on timing: I do not think a pending redefinition is a reason to wait, because the discovery is established independently of any decision by the metrology bodies. I would, however, like a dissenting view on whether Ye is better credited for the clock itself or for the clock-comb integration, since the citation should state the former.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B042 first, calling the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp triple a fair and clean configuration with fifteen years of confirmation, and sees B037 as sound but affected by Ye's earlier 2005 prize, which he says does not exclude recognition but may colour the committee's view.
responses.response: On B037 we agree that Ye's earlier prize is a perception issue rather than a bar, and I would resist letting it weigh against the lattice-clock work, which stands on its own. On B042 I disagree that the configuration is clean. Eriksson, Lindroth, Mehlig and Olsson each flag that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that actually motivated the HgTe experiment is outside the three names, Zhang is deceased, and the three-dimensional topological insulator work by Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore and Balents, and Hasan is not represented. Kane and Mele are decisive as theorists, but the experimental observation followed a proposal the credit list leaves out, and the 2016 prize on topological phases lies nearby. I take B042 seriously, since five members placed it in their top three, and I keep it as an alternative, but I would want the committee to settle the BHZ question before treating the trio as fair.

responses.point: Mehlig places active-matter hydrodynamics (B005) first as one of the strongest conceptual advances in recent statistical physics, with three distinct contributions mapped to Vicsek, Toner and Ramaswamy, while acknowledging that Yuhai Tu's role in the Toner-Tu theory cannot be resolved from the supplied names.
responses.response: This is a conceptually appealing case and I respect the argument that flocking evades the Mermin-Wagner restriction through nonlinear fluctuations, which is a genuine theoretical insight. My hesitation is the one Mehlig names himself. Omitting Tu from a theory called Toner-Tu is a structural defect in the credit, not a detail, and the exact 2D exponents are still debated experimentally. I also note that no other member ranked B005, so the opening evidence does not show it has the cross-field support needed to carry a prize this year. I would be interested in whether Mehlig sees the Vicsek model and the continuum theory as one achievement or two, because that decides whether a three-name list can honestly be defended.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B037 first, describing the clock physics (magic wavelengths, shifts, many-body control) as clean and well understood, and the credit as supporting a compact two-person prize with only a modest allocation debate, possibly overdue given the adjacent 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I agree and I rely on her atomic-structure reading, which I cannot make myself. Her point that the physics is well understood is part of why I rank it ahead of the more dynamic fields. Where I would add a qualification is her suggestion that ion-clock and comb communities are already recognised elsewhere and so are not a concern: the committee should say explicitly in the citation what is being honoured, namely the lattice scheme and its realisation at 10^-18, so that the prize is not read as a general award for optical clocks that passes over the Al+ and ion groups.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the lattice clock sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether Ye is best credited for the clock performance or for clock-comb integration, and how much weight the NIST, PTB and other lattice-clock groups deserve.
Whether the Higgs observation (B006) can be given a defensible three-person form, for example by an expert view on which individuals are the decisive discoverers across ATLAS and CMS.
Whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission makes B042 impractical as a three-person prize or whether a different credit set is allowed.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My documented connections are my PhD supervisor David Gross, my early mentor Hector Rubinstein, my co-author Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theoretical-physics group, and none of them is among the credited names on the shortlisted ballots. My own field is theoretical high-energy physics and cosmology, so I have no subject-matter proximity to the lattice clock, but also less ability to judge its experimental priority history.
